lines.text: being. It is for those who realize that nothing can be forced
and who wait patiently for God, as the Psalmist says, "to
bring forth their vindication as the light" and their "right
as the noonday" (Ps. 37: 6).
LII
Thus it is those who wait upon God who are extolled in
the first group of beatitudes. Four beatitudes follow which
suggest how a genuine attitude of waiting bears fruit and
must become a living power in man's life. For those who
know how to wait upon God, the being of man is released
from the present, from the given, from its connexion with
what he has and is. It turns towards the future, towards what
God will grant, what God will make of man. Thus man is
released for all the encounters which God will send him and
in which God's future will come to meet him.
"Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy."
This does not need many words of explanation; we need
only point out that the word translated "merciful" has in
truth a wider meaning; it implies not only compassion but
(in general) goodness, active beneficent love. Blessed are
they whose heart is inspired by such creative goodness. They
shall obtain mercy. Yes, they are privileged to perceive the
mercy of God active towards them in that they are allowed
to experience how the man who is not embittered despite
poverty, pain, and unfulfilled longing, the man who is
readily accessible to the pain and sorrow of his neighbour-
how such a one easily bears his own sorrows.
"Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God."
Who is pure in heart? What is meant is the disposition of
honesty, of inner truthfulness, which refuses to impose either
on itself or others, which hates all pretence and falsity; the
honourableness and openness of disposition which has no
unconfessed ulterior motives, which will not adopt a pose
but offers itself in spontaneous naturalness to others. What
we call purity in a more specialized sense is included in this
